title: Candy Corn Bag

drivers.name: Halloween (event week)
drivers.evidence: Noise-adjusted multiplier x2.65 from 3 past occurrences; consistent lift around Halloween.

drivers.name: Price increase (+6%)
drivers.evidence: Price is now 6% above regular; past promotions show limited lift even at 30% off (x1.45 avg). A price increase likely reduces demand, especially without a promotion.

drivers.name: Supplier delivery short
drivers.evidence: Supplier warning implies supply risk; may limit units available for sale, reducing actual demand observed.

adjustment.analysis: Halloween drives a strong seasonal lift (noise-adjusted x2.65). The price increase to $4.08 (+6%) may dampen demand, but the historical promotion data shows price cuts (even 30% off) only lift sales x1.45 on average, and the current price is not a promotion. The supplier warning of short delivery introduces supply risk, which may reduce sell-through. The classical uplift model’s x2.65 is a good starting point, but the price increase and supply risk suggest a downward adjustment. No recent promotion or trend supports a higher lift. Evidence is solid for Halloween, weaker for price and supply. Adjust down from model's suggestion.

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 10.3 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 24.2 | 10%-90%: 0.0 - 19.0

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-85% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
